blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Unit 4 (Differential Equations), arranged by the unit's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation that shows the working.
4.1 Differential equations: Definition, Order and Degree

blocks.prompt: 1 Which one of the following is a differential equation?
blocks.explanation: A differential equation must contain at least one derivative of the dependent variable. Only \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^{2} + y\) contains a derivative; the other three are ordinary equations.

book_ref.quote: An equation that involves at least one derivative of a dependent variable with respect to an independent variable is called a differential equation

blocks.prompt: 2 Why is \(y = \sin x + 4\) not a differential equation?

options.text: No derivative of y appears in it
y is not a function of x

blocks.explanation: A differential equation must involve at least one derivative. This equation has no derivative, so it is not a differential equation (the sine and the constant do not matter).

book_ref.quote: is not a differential equation, because no derivative appears in it

blocks.prompt: 3 In the differential equation \(\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 5Q\), the dependent variable is:
blocks.explanation: In \(\frac{dQ}{dt}\) the quantity being differentiated, \(Q\), is the dependent variable; \(t\) is the independent variable.

book_ref.quote: is the independent variable (we choose it freely)

blocks.prompt: 4 A differential equation is called an ordinary differential equation when:

options.text: It has only one independent variable

blocks.explanation: \"Ordinary\" means only one independent variable, so only ordinary derivatives such as \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\) appear. It has nothing to do with the order or degree.

book_ref.quote: means there is only one independent variable, so only ordinary derivatives

blocks.prompt: 5 If \(v = \dfrac{ds}{dt}\) and \(a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}\), then the acceleration \(a\) in terms of \(s\) is:
blocks.explanation: \(a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right) = \frac{d^{2}s}{dt^{2}}\), the second derivative of \(s\). Squaring the first derivative is a different thing.

book_ref.quote: For example, if a particle covers a distance

blocks.prompt: 6 The order of the differential equation \(\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + 4\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3} - y = x\) is:
blocks.explanation: The highest derivative present is \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\), of order 2. The power 3 belongs to the first derivative and does not decide the order.

book_ref.quote: The order of a differential equation is the order of the highest derivative that appears in the differential equation.

blocks.prompt: 7 The degree of the differential equation \(\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + 4\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3} - y = x\) is:
blocks.explanation: The degree is the power of the highest-order derivative only. \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\) appears to the power 1, so the degree is 1 (the cube is on a lower derivative).

book_ref.quote: The degree of a differential equation is the greatest exponent of the highest-order derivative appearing in the differential equation.

blocks.prompt: 8 The order and degree of \(\left(\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}\right)^{2} + x\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\) are respectively:
blocks.explanation: Highest derivative: \(\frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}\), so order 3. It is raised to the power 2, so degree 2.

book_ref.quote: Look at every derivative in the equation and take the largest such number.

blocks.prompt: 9 The degree of the differential equation \(\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + e^{dy/dx} = x\) is:
blocks.explanation: The derivative \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) sits inside an exponential, so the equation cannot be written as a polynomial in its derivatives; the degree is not defined (the order is 2).

book_ref.quote: If a derivative is stuck inside sin, cos, log, an exponential, etc., the degree is not defined

blocks.prompt: 10 The degree of \(\sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\) is:
blocks.explanation: Square both sides: \(1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2} = \left(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\right)^{2}\). The highest derivative \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\) now has power 2, so the degree is 2.

book_ref.quote: First clear any root or fractional power that contains a derivative

blocks.prompt: 11 The degree of \(3\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}} + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{4} - xy = 0\) is:
blocks.explanation: The highest derivative is \(\frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}\) and it appears to the power 1, so the degree is 1. The power 4 is on a lower derivative.

book_ref.quote: Taking the largest power anywhere as the degree

blocks.prompt: 12 Which one of the following is a first-order differential equation?
blocks.explanation: Order 1 means the highest derivative is \(\frac{dy}{dx}\). Only the first equation has no second or third derivative (its degree is 2, but its order is 1).

book_ref.quote: A differential equation of order 1 is called a first-order differential equation

blocks.prompt: 13 The order and degree of \(\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \left(x + \dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{1/2}\) are respectively:
blocks.explanation: Square both sides to clear the root: \(\left(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\right)^{2} = x + \frac{dy}{dx}\). The highest derivative is of order 2 and now appears squared: order 2, degree 2.

book_ref.quote: First-order differential equations (order 1) are the subject of this unit.

blocks.text: 4.1.1 Construction of First-Order and Differential Equations from Practical Situations

blocks.prompt: 14 A quantity \(Q\) changes at a rate proportional to \(Q\) itself. The differential equation is:
blocks.explanation: \"Rate of change of \(Q\)\" is \(\frac{dQ}{dt}\) and \"proportional to \(Q\)\" means \"\(= k \times Q\)\". So \(\frac{dQ}{dt} = kQ\).

book_ref.quote: First-order differential equations model problems where the rate of change of a quantity depends on the quantity itself or on time.

blocks.prompt: 15 A medicine is removed from the blood at a rate proportional to the amount \(A\) present. With \(k > 0\), the model is:
blocks.explanation: The amount decreases, so its rate is negative: \(\frac{dA}{dt} = -kA\) with \(k > 0\).

book_ref.quote: Decide the sign: if the quantity is decreasing, its rate is negative

blocks.prompt: 16 The volume \(V\) of water in a leaking tank decreases at a rate proportional to \(\sqrt{V}\). With \(k > 0\), the differential equation is:
blocks.explanation: Rate of change \(\frac{dV}{dt}\); proportional to \(\sqrt{V}\) gives \(k\sqrt{V}\); decreasing gives the minus sign: \(\frac{dV}{dt} = -k\sqrt{V}\).

book_ref.quote: from a situation is a translation job

blocks.prompt: 17 In the model \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = kP\) for a population, the population remains constant when:
blocks.explanation: If \(k = 0\), then \(\frac{dP}{dt} = 0\), so \(P\) does not change. \(k > 0\) gives growth and \(k < 0\) gives decay.

book_ref.quote: The rate of change of a population is proportional to the population itself.

blocks.prompt: 18 In the price model \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = kP\) (\(P > 0\)), deflation corresponds to:
blocks.explanation: Deflation means the price decreases, so \(\frac{dP}{dt} < 0\). With \(P > 0\) this needs \(k < 0\).

book_ref.quote: Inflation means the price of goods is increasing over time, while deflation means the price of goods is decreasing over time.

blocks.prompt: 19 With \(k > 0\), Newton's law of cooling or heating for a body at temperature \(T\) in surroundings at constant temperature \(T_{S}\) is:
blocks.explanation: The rate is proportional to the difference, and with \(k > 0\) the bracket must be \(T_{S} - T\) so that a hot body cools. \(k(T - T_{S})\) would make a hot body hotter.

book_ref.quote: the rate of change of the body's temperature with respect to time is proportional to the difference between the body's temperature and the surrounding temperature

blocks.prompt: 20 In \(\dfrac{dT}{dt} = k(T_{S} - T)\) with \(k > 0\), if \(T > T_{S}\) then:
blocks.explanation: \(T_{S} - T < 0\) and \(k > 0\), so \(\frac{dT}{dt} < 0\): the body is cooling down.

book_ref.quote: the body is cooling down and

blocks.prompt: 21 A pie at \(70^{\circ}\)C is in a room at \(20^{\circ}\)C, and \(\dfrac{dT}{dt} = k(T_{S} - T)\) with \(k = 0.1\) per minute. At that moment \(\dfrac{dT}{dt}\) is:
blocks.explanation: \(\frac{dT}{dt} = 0.1(20 - 70) = 0.1(-50) = -5\) degrees per minute; negative, so the pie is cooling.

book_ref.quote: so the tea cools, exactly as in real life

blocks.prompt: 22 In an RC circuit, the voltage across a capacitor of capacitance \(C\) carrying charge \(q\) is:
blocks.explanation: A capacitor's voltage is charge divided by capacitance: \(V_{C} = \frac{q}{C}\).

book_ref.quote: The voltage across the capacitor is

blocks.prompt: 23 In the RC circuit model, the current \(I\) and the charge \(q\) are related by:
blocks.explanation: Current is the rate of flow of charge, \(I = \frac{dq}{dt}\). This substitution turns the circuit law into a differential equation in \(q\).

book_ref.quote: current is the rate of flow of charge

blocks.prompt: 24 For a resistor \(R\) and capacitor \(C\) in series with a source of emf \(V_{S}\), Kirchhoff's voltage law gives:
blocks.explanation: \(V_{S} = V_{R} + V_{C} = IR + \frac{q}{C}\) and \(I = \frac{dq}{dt}\), so \(R\frac{dq}{dt} + \frac{q}{C} = V_{S}\).

book_ref.quote: By Kirchhoff's voltage law, the sum of the voltages across the resistor and capacitor equals the total voltage from the battery

blocks.prompt: 25 The voltage across an inductor of inductance \(L\) carrying current \(I\) is:
blocks.explanation: An inductor's voltage is proportional to how fast the current changes: \(V_{L} = L\frac{dI}{dt}\). (\(RI\) is the resistor's voltage.)

book_ref.quote: an inductor opposes a change of current; its voltage is proportional to how fast the current changes

blocks.prompt: 26 The RL circuit model \(L\dfrac{dI}{dt} + RI = V_{S}\) can be written as:
blocks.explanation: Move \(RI\) across: \(L\frac{dI}{dt} = V_{S} - RI\); divide by \(L\): \(\frac{dI}{dt} = \frac{V_{S} - RI}{L}\).

book_ref.quote: The sum of the voltages across the resistor and inductor equals the applied voltage

blocks.prompt: 27 For the model \(RC\dfrac{dq}{dt} = CV_{S} - q\), the order and degree are respectively:
blocks.explanation: Only the first derivative \(\frac{dq}{dt}\) appears, to the power 1: order 1, degree 1.

book_ref.quote: All these are first-order, first-degree differential equations.

blocks.text: 4.2 Solution of First-Order and First-Degree Differential Equations

blocks.prompt: 28 The general form of a first-order, first-degree differential equation is:
blocks.explanation: First order: only \(\frac{dy}{dx}\); first degree: \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) to the power 1. So the equation can be solved for \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\).

book_ref.quote: General form of the first order and first degree differential equations.

blocks.prompt: 29 If \(M(x, y)\,dx + N(x, y)\,dy = 0\) with \(N \ne 0\), then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) equals:
blocks.explanation: \(N\,dy = -M\,dx\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{M}{N}\).

book_ref.quote: It is always possible to write the above equation in differential form as follows:

blocks.prompt: 30 In differential form, \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2x - y}{x + 3y}\) is:
blocks.explanation: Cross-multiply: \((x + 3y)\,dy = (2x - y)\,dx\). Bring all terms to one side: \((2x - y)\,dx - (x + 3y)\,dy = 0\); the moved term changes sign.

book_ref.quote: where \(M(x, y)\) and \(N(x, y)\) are the functions of \(x\) and \(y\).

blocks.prompt: 31 A differential equation together with a condition \(y(x_{0}) = y_{0}\) is called:
blocks.explanation: A differential equation together with an initial value condition \(y(x_{0}) = y_{0}\) is an Initial Value Problem (IVP).

book_ref.quote: A differential equation together with an initial value condition is called an Initial Value Problem (IVP).

blocks.prompt: 32 The initial value condition \(y(2) = 5\) means:
blocks.explanation: \(y(x_{0}) = y_{0}\) means \(y = y_{0}\) at \(x = x_{0}\). So \(y(2) = 5\) means \(y = 5\) when \(x = 2\); it is not a product.

book_ref.quote: is called an initial value condition or one point boundary condition.

blocks.prompt: 33 The general solution of a first-order differential equation contains:
blocks.explanation: The general solution of a first-order equation contains one arbitrary constant; each value of the constant gives one curve of the family.

book_ref.quote: The general solution contains one arbitrary constant; it is a family of curves.

blocks.prompt: 34 The solution of the IVP \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^{2}\), \(y(1) = 4\) is:

book_ref.quote: In an IVP, first find the general solution, then substitute

blocks.prompt: 35 Which function is a solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2y\)?
blocks.explanation: For \(y = 5e^{2x}\): \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 10e^{2x} = 2(5e^{2x}) = 2y\), an identity. The others fail, e.g. \(y = 2e^{x}\) gives \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 2e^{x} \ne 4e^{x}\).

book_ref.quote: A solution of a differential equation is a function defined on some interval

blocks.explanation: \(x^{2}y^{3} = g(x)h(y)\) with \(g = x^{2}\), \(h = y^{3}\). The sums \(x + y\), \(x^{2} + y\) and \(\sin(x + y)\) cannot be split into (only \(x\)) \(\times\) (only \(y\)).

book_ref.quote: A first-order, first-degree differential equation is called Separable if it can be written as:

blocks.prompt: 39 The general solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2xy\) is (\(A\) an arbitrary constant):
blocks.explanation: \(\frac{dy}{y} = 2x\,dx\), so \(\ln|y| = x^{2} + c\) and \(y = Ae^{x^{2}}\) with \(A = \pm e^{c}\).

blocks.prompt: 40 The general solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin y}\) is:
blocks.explanation: \(\sin y\,dy = \cos x\,dx\), so \(-\cos y = \sin x + c_{1}\), i.e. \(\sin x + \cos y = c\).

book_ref.quote: We can separate the variables: put everything with

blocks.prompt: 41 The general solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 + y^{2}\) is:

book_ref.quote: Method: separate, integrate both sides, add one constant.

blocks.prompt: 42 After integrating both sides of a separable equation we may get \(+c_{1}\) on the left and \(+c_{2}\) on the right. We write only one constant because:

options.text: they combine into one constant \(c = c_{2} - c_{1}\)
the left side has no constant of integration

blocks.explanation: Moving \(c_{1}\) to the right gives \(c_{2} - c_{1}\), which is again just one arbitrary constant \(c\).

book_ref.quote: moving them together gives a single constant

blocks.prompt: 43 Besides its general solution, the equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x(y - 2)\) has the constant solution:
blocks.explanation: Here \(h(y) = y - 2\) vanishes at \(y = 2\). For \(y = 2\): \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 0 = x(2 - 2)\), so \(y = 2\) is a solution.

book_ref.quote: Small caution: dividing by

blocks.prompt: 44 The family \(x^{2} + 4y^{2} = c\) is the general solution of:
blocks.explanation: Differentiate: \(2x + 8y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{2x}{8y} = -\frac{x}{4y}\).

book_ref.quote: Check by differentiating the answer: you must get the original equation back.

blocks.prompt: 46 The solution of the IVP \(x\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y\) (\(x > 0\)), \(y(1) = 3\) is:
blocks.explanation: \(\frac{dy}{y} = \frac{dx}{x}\) gives \(\ln|y| = \ln|x| + \ln|c|\), so \(y = cx\). Then \(3 = c(1)\): \(y = 3x\).

book_ref.quote: Integrating a side that still contains both

blocks.prompt: 47 Which one of the following differential equations is homogeneous?
blocks.explanation: Every term of \(x^{2} + y^{2}\) and of \(xy\) has degree 2; dividing by \(x^{2}\) gives \(\frac{1 + (y/x)^{2}}{y/x} = F\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\). The other three mix degrees.

book_ref.quote: A first-order, first degree differential equation is called Homogeneous if it can be written in the form

blocks.prompt: 48 To solve a homogeneous differential equation, the substitution used is:
blocks.explanation: Put \(y = vx\) where \(v\) is a function of \(x\); by the product rule \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\). Writing only \(v\) forgets the second term.

book_ref.quote: can be converted into a separable differential equation in variables

blocks.prompt: 49 With \(y = vx\), the right side of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x^{3} + y^{3}}{x^{2}y}\) becomes:
blocks.explanation: Replace \(x\) by 1 and \(y\) by \(v\): \(\frac{1 + v^{3}}{1 \cdot v} = \frac{1 + v^{3}}{v}\). (Directly: \(\frac{x^{3}(1 + v^{3})}{x^{3}v}\).)

book_ref.quote: can easily be simplified by replacing

blocks.prompt: 50 For \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = F\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)\), after putting \(y = vx\) the separable form is:
blocks.explanation: \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = F(v)\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = F(v) - v\) and \(\frac{dv}{F(v) - v} = \frac{dx}{x}\). Forgetting to subtract \(v\) is a common slip.

book_ref.quote: It becomes separable differential equation.

blocks.explanation: \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1 - v}{1 + v}\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1 - v - v - v^{2}}{1 + v} = \frac{1 - 2v - v^{2}}{1 + v}\).

book_ref.quote: Substituting the values of

blocks.prompt: 54 The general solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x} + \tan\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)\) is:
blocks.explanation: \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \tan v\), so \(\frac{\cos v}{\sin v}dv = \frac{dx}{x}\), \(\ln|\sin v| = \ln|x| + \ln|c|\), giving \(\sin\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = cx\).

blocks.prompt: 55 A student puts \(y = vx\) in a homogeneous equation and writes \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v\). The mistake is:

options.text: \(v\) is a function of \(x\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx}\)

book_ref.quote: is the most common error in this topic

blocks.explanation: The constant 1 has degree 0 while \(x\) and \(y\) have degree 1, so it is not a function of \(\frac{y}{x}\) alone; and the sums cannot be split as \(g(x)h(y)\).

blocks.text: 4.3 Applications of First Order Differential Equations in Real-Life Problems

blocks.prompt: 57 A population obeys \(N = N_{0}e^{kt}\) and doubles every 5 hours. Then \(k\) is:

book_ref.quote: the population grows at a rate proportional to its size

blocks.prompt: 58 If \(e^{4k} = 3\), then \(k\) equals:
blocks.explanation: Take \(\ln\) of both sides: \(4k = \ln 3\), so \(k = \frac{1}{4}\ln 3\).

book_ref.quote: If \(e^{ak} = b\), then \(ak = \ln b\), so \(k = \frac{1}{a}\ln b\).

blocks.prompt: 59 A radioactive substance has decay constant \(k = 0.0231\) per year. Its half-life is about:

book_ref.quote: So the half-life does not depend on the starting mass.

blocks.prompt: 60 A radioactive sample of 64 g has a half-life of 6 hours. The mass left after 18 hours is:
blocks.explanation: 18 hours is 3 half-lives: \(64 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3} = 8\) g.

book_ref.quote: Half-life is the time required for a quantity of a radioactive substance to reduce to half of its initial amount due to radioactive decay.

blocks.prompt: 61 In the decay model \(\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM\), the constant \(k\) satisfies:
blocks.explanation: The minus sign already shows the decrease; for the mass to decrease, \(k\) must be positive (the decay constant).

book_ref.quote: radioactive mass decays at a rate proportional to the mass present

blocks.prompt: 62 An economy has deflation of 5% per year. The model for the price \(P\) (\(t\) in years) is:
blocks.explanation: Deflation: price falls, so a minus sign; 5% is written as 0.05. Hence \(\frac{dP}{dt} = -0.05P\).

book_ref.quote: A percentage rate is written as a decimal

blocks.prompt: 63 With inflation of 6% per year (continuous model), an item now costing Rs. 2000 will cost after 4 years about:

book_ref.quote: Growth (bacteria, money, inflation)

blocks.explanation: As \(t \to \infty\), \(e^{-0.03t} \to 0\), so \(T \to 25\), the room temperature.

blocks.explanation: As \(t \to \infty\), \(e^{-t/(RC)} \to 0\), so \(q \to CV_{S} = 2 \times 10 = 20\) coulombs.

book_ref.quote: Decay (radioactive mass, deflation)
